extracted.intended_audience: donors, potential grantee charities, and philanthropic evaluators (people interested in GiveWell's top-charity selection process)
extracted.subtask_description: GiveWell's documented process for finding, evaluating, and recommending top charities that work on priority programs for the global poor. Covers eligibility, investigative methods, substantive evaluation criteria (evidence, cost-effectiveness, room for more funding, transparency), and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility (focus on priority programs)
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to be eligible for "top charity" status, a charity must be explicitly focused on one or more of our priority programs, such as distributing insecticide-treated nets to prevent malaria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These programs represent, according to GiveWell's research, the most evidence-backed approaches to helping the global poor. See GiveWell's published criteria for priority programs. The eligibility requirement filters which organizations are considered for deeper investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength and rigor of evidence (Does it work?)
rubrics_metrics.description: We look for highly rigorous evidence connecting aid activities to improved life outcomes; GiveWell finds this evidence primarily in academic literature rather than in charities' internal self-evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations deepen understanding of the evidence base, examining strengths and weaknesses of key studies and whether results generalize to larger-scale programs. See GiveWell's 'Our Principles for Assessing Evidence', 'How We Evaluate a Study', and 'Surveying the Research on a Topic'. Anti-pattern: relying solely on internal self-evaluations, which rarely provide rigorous causal evidence of life-outcome impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of implementation and charity-specific execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the charity is carrying out the program with high quality and whether the organization adds substantial value relative to what the program would look like without its presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine charity-specific data such as internal reports and interviews with charity representatives. Large-scale aid projects often require coordination with many actors, so GiveWell aims to understand the charity's specific role thoroughly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness (What do you get for your dollar?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to quantify the impact of the program as executed (not just in studies), using measures such as cost per life saved or financial benefits to recipients per dollar spent by donors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These estimates involve substantial judgment; GiveWell publishes the details and major assumptions so readers can adjust them. Estimates are not advised to be taken literally; their purpose is to (a) identify robust differences that affect rankings and (b) surface critical questions about activities. See GiveWell's cost-effectiveness page for methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Room for more funding (marginal impact of additional dollars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand how additional funding will impact the organization — specifically the effect of marginal dollars — because GiveWell expects recommendations to lead to increased funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek charities that can use more funding productively. GiveWell has withdrawn recommendations in the past when a charity had raised as much funding as it could productively absorb. Assess funding gaps and marginal absorptive capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and willingness to share information
rubrics_metrics.description: A charity’s willingness to share information with GiveWell and the public so its work can be assessed is an important part of the evaluation process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GiveWell publishes as much as it can from investigations — notes from conversations, site visit notes and photos, original documents, and analysis details — and prefers charities that help enable this transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability / external validity of study evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating evidence from studies, GiveWell examines considerations regarding how likely study results are to generalize to larger-scale programs and different contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deepen investigation of the evidence base to evaluate external validity. Consider differences between trial conditions and real-world scale-ups when estimating impact and cost-effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operation effectiveness at scale / track record with substantial funding
rubrics_metrics.description: One criterion (from GiveWell's August 2022 clarification) is that the program/charity has been directed a significant amount of money and has been seen to operate effectively at scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of effective operation at scale supports confidence that additional donor funds will translate to predictable impact rather than only discrete study results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood of significant impact (preference for high-likelihood gains)
rubrics_metrics.description: GiveWell prioritizes programs where there is a high likelihood of significant impact from funding the program (as opposed to low-likelihood, enormous-impact bets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects a preference for interventions with relatively certain, substantial returns per dollar rather than speculative, low-probability high-return opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary case should rest on direct impact rather than information value
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, the overwhelming case for funding should rest on the direct impact of a grant, not on the value of information that might be gathered through the grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grants made mainly for learning or information value are less likely to motivate a top-charity recommendation unless the direct-impact case is strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program has funding gaps that meet GiveWell's cost-effectiveness bar
rubrics_metrics.description: A program should have funding gaps that meet GiveWell's current cost-effectiveness threshold, indicating that incremental funding would be a cost-effective use of donor dollars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of deciding to recommend a charity is confirming that there exist actionable funding opportunities that Clear cost-effectiveness calculations identify as competitively high-value relative to GiveWell's bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritization/funnel approach to selecting programs and charities
rubrics_metrics.description: GiveWell conducts short, shallow reviews of a large number of programs and then prioritizes more intensive reviews only for programs that seem more promising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs and organizations are assessed for prioritization based on strength of evidence, cost-effectiveness, and room for more funding. The funnel concentrates in-depth resources on the most promising opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of diverse investigation methods and information sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Most investigation consists of conversations with charity representatives and review of their documents; GiveWell also speaks to other funders and typically conducts at least one site visit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with transparency, GiveWell shares investigation materials publicly. Sources include charity internal reports, interviews, other funders, site visit notes and photos, and external academic literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up, engagement, and post-grant learning (lookbacks)
rubrics_metrics.description: GiveWell follows up intensively with top charities over time, expecting engagement that allows them to deepen understanding of activities and progress and to learn from both positive and negative developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GiveWell conducts lookbacks on some grants to compare outcomes to original assessments (examples: New Incentives and Helen Keller Intl) and treats a charity's willingness to share struggles and outcomes as a strength.
